evals.prompt:
I have these markdown notes from my IoT water quality monitoring project. Can you turn them into a proper LaTeX report?

# Introduction

## Background
Water quality monitoring is essential for public health. Traditional methods involve manual sampling which is time-consuming and error-prone. IoT-based systems can automate this process using sensors for pH, turbidity, dissolved oxygen, and temperature.

## Problem Statement
Rural communities in Kenya lack access to real-time water quality data, leading to waterborne disease outbreaks.

## Objectives
1. Design an IoT-based water quality monitoring system using Arduino and ESP32
2. Develop a web dashboard for real-time data visualization using React
3. Implement threshold-based alerts for contamination detection

## Significance
This system could reduce waterborne disease cases by enabling early detection of contamination.

## Scope
Limited to freshwater sources (rivers and wells) in Kiambu County. Only pH, turbidity, DO, and temperature sensors are used.

# Literature Review

## IoT in Environmental Monitoring
Smith et al. (2023) developed a LoRa-based water monitoring system achieving 95% data transmission reliability. Kumar and Patel (2022) compared WiFi vs cellular IoT architectures for remote monitoring.

## Water Quality Parameters
pH, turbidity, dissolved oxygen, and temperature are the four primary indicators (WHO, 2024).

# Methodology

## System Architecture
The system uses a three-tier architecture: sensor layer, gateway layer, and cloud layer.

## Hardware Design
- Arduino Mega for sensor data acquisition
- ESP32 for WiFi connectivity
- pH sensor module (SEN0161)
- Turbidity sensor (SEN0189)

## Software Stack
- Backend: Node.js with Express
- Frontend: React with Chart.js
- Database: MongoDB

# Results

The system successfully monitored water quality parameters over a 30-day trial period. pH readings had an accuracy of ±0.1 compared to lab measurements. Turbidity sensor showed 92% correlation with standard nephelometric methods.

# Conclusion
The IoT-based water quality monitoring system demonstrated feasibility for rural deployment. The low-cost design (total BOM < $150) makes it accessible for community-level implementation.

Project code: EN-PRO-25-01
Authors: JOHN DOE (ENE241-0100/2021), JANE SMITH (ENE241-0101/2021)
Supervisor: Dr. JAMES MWANGI
Department: DEPARTMENT OF ELECTRICAL AND ELECTRONIC ENGINEERING
Degree: BACHELOR OF SCIENCE IN ELECTRICAL AND ELECTRONIC ENGINEERING
evals.expected_output: A complete set of LaTeX files (main.tex + chapter files in structure/) following the JKUAT UPRO template, with the correct title page using HDlogo, proper front matter sections, and all markdown content converted to appropriate LaTeX formatting.

I need to format my final year project notes into a JKUAT report. Here's my content in markdown format. The project is about solar panel efficiency optimization using MPPT algorithms.

# Solar Panel MPPT Optimization

## Abstract
This project investigates Maximum Power Point Tracking (MPPT) algorithms for photovoltaic systems. We compared Perturb & Observe (P&O), Incremental Conductance (IC), and a proposed fuzzy logic-based MPPT controller. Simulation results in MATLAB/Simulink show the fuzzy controller achieves 98.5% tracking efficiency compared to 94.2% for P&O and 96.1% for IC under variable irradiance conditions.

## Chapter 1: Introduction
### 1.1 Background
Kenya's Vision 2030 targets 100% renewable energy access. Solar PV installations are growing at 15% annually but efficiency losses due to partial shading and rapid irradiance changes remain a challenge.

### 1.2 Problem Statement
Conventional MPPT algorithms oscillate around the MPP under rapidly changing conditions, causing up to 8% power loss.

### 1.3 Objectives
- To model a PV system with boost converter in MATLAB/Simulink
- To implement and compare P&O, IC, and fuzzy logic MPPT algorithms
- To evaluate tracking efficiency under standard and variable irradiance profiles

## Chapter 2: Literature Review
### 2.1 PV Cell Modeling
The single-diode model is widely used (Villalva et al., 2009). The I-V characteristic is given by:

I = I_ph - I_0 * (exp((V + I*Rs)/(n*Vt)) - 1) - (V + I*Rs)/Rsh

### 2.2 MPPT Techniques
P&O is the most common due to simplicity (Femia et al., 2005). IC offers better performance under rapidly changing conditions (Safari & Mekhilef, 2011). Fuzzy logic controllers have shown superior tracking in recent studies (Bouselham et al., 2017).

## Chapter 3: Methodology
### 3.1 PV Array Model
We modeled a 250W polycrystalline panel (Vmpp=30.2V, Impp=8.28A) using the single-diode model.

### 3.2 Boost Converter Design
Input voltage: 24-36V, Output voltage: 48V, Switching frequency: 50kHz
- Inductance: L = V_in * D / (f * ΔI_L) = 470µH
- Capacitance: C = I_out * D / (f * ΔV_out) = 220µF

### 3.3 Fuzzy Logic Controller
Inputs: Error (E) and Change in Error (CE)
Output: Change in duty cycle (ΔD)
Membership functions: 7 triangular MFs for each variable
Rule base: 49 rules

## Chapter 4: Results
### Tracking Efficiency Comparison
| Algorithm | Steady State | Dynamic | Overall |
|-----------|-------------|---------|----------|
| P&O | 96.1% | 89.3% | 94.2% |
| IC | 97.5% | 93.2% | 96.1% |
| Fuzzy | 99.1% | 97.8% | 98.5% |

### Response Time
The fuzzy controller reached MPP in 0.15s compared to 0.45s for P&O.

## Conclusion
The fuzzy logic MPPT controller outperformed conventional algorithms by 2-4% in overall tracking efficiency.
